records.source: בִּשְׁנַת֙ שְׁבַֽע־עֶשְׂרֵ֣ה שָׁנָ֔ה לְפֶ֖קַח בֶּן־רְמַלְיָ֑הוּ מָלַ֛ךְ אָחָ֥ז בֶּן־יוֹתָ֖ם מֶ֥לֶךְ יְהוּדָֽה׃
records.gloss: In [the] year seventeen year of Pekah son of Remaliah reigned Ahaz son of Jotham king of Judah.
pieces: In the seventeenth year of Pekah son of Remaliah, Ahaz son of Jotham became king of Judah.

L.1: In the seventeenth year of Pekah son of Remaliah, Ahaz son of Jotham, king of Judah, reigned.

R.1: Ahaz son of Jotham became king of Judah. It was the seventeenth year that Pekah son of Remaliah had been king of Israel.

decisions.choice: dated by the reign of Pekah, king of Israel
decisions.reason: As throughout Kings, the start of a reign in Judah is dated by the year of the king ruling in Israel (1 Kings 15:1). Pekah had seized the throne of Israel in Samaria (15:25). Ahaz's reign is told in verses 1-20, and again in 2 Chronicles 28.

decisions.choice: Ahaz ... king of Judah: the title belongs to Ahaz
decisions.reason: "King of Judah" describes Ahaz, who now begins to reign, not his father Jotham. The verb "reigned" with a date marks the start of the reign, as in 1 Kings 15:1.

decisions.choice: Ahaz son of Jotham: the king of Isaiah 7
decisions.reason: This is the Ahaz whom the prophet Isaiah met in the crisis of verse 5 (Isaiah 7:1-17), and to whom he gave the sign of Immanuel.

decisions.choice: two sentences, the date second
decisions.reason: Readable splits the formula into two sentences, as these books allow, and says that Pekah was king of Israel.

records.heading: Ahaz king of Judah

records.source: בֶּן־עֶשְׂרִ֤ים שָׁנָה֙ אָחָ֣ז בְּמָלְכ֔וֹ וְשֵׁשׁ־עֶשְׂרֵ֣ה שָׁנָ֔ה מָלַ֖ךְ בִּירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וְלֹא־עָשָׂ֣ה הַיָּשָׁ֗ר בְּעֵינֵ֛י יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהָ֖יו כְּדָוִ֥ד אָבִֽיו׃
records.gloss: A son of twenty year[s] [was] Ahaz when he became king, and sixteen year[s] he reigned in Jerusalem; and not he did the right in [the] eyes of Yahweh his God like David his father.
pieces: Ahaz was twenty years old when he became king, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. He did not do what was right in the sight of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} his God, as his ancestor David had done.

L.2: Ahaz [was] twenty years old when he became king, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. And he did not do the right in [the] eyes of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} his God, like David his father.

R.2: Ahaz was twenty years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for sixteen years. He did not do what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} his God said was right, as his ancestor David had done.

decisions.choice: a son of twenty years: twenty years old
decisions.reason: Hebrew gives a person's age as being "a son of" so many years.

decisions.choice: twenty years old, sixteen years: numbers hard to fit together
alternatives: twenty-five years old (some Greek copies of 2 Chronicles 28:1)
decisions.reason: Ahaz's son Hezekiah was twenty-five when he became king after him (18:2). If Ahaz was twenty at his accession and reigned sixteen years, he would have been about eleven when Hezekiah was born. Reigns that overlapped with a father's, or an error in copying one of the numbers, may explain this. 2 Chronicles 28:1 has the same numbers in Hebrew, but some ancient Greek copies there read twenty-five. Every level keeps the numbers of the Hebrew text; reviewers should check the evidence.

decisions.choice: no mother named
decisions.reason: The formula for a king of Judah usually names his mother (15:2, 33). For Ahaz it names none. The text gives no reason.

decisions.choice: he did not do what was right ... like David: the good verdict denied
decisions.reason: The verdict is the one given to the good kings of Judah (1 Kings 15:11), turned into a denial. His father Jotham and the kings before him had received the good verdict (15:3, 34). "David his father" means his ancestor David, the measure for every king of Judah.

decisions.choice: did not do the right in [the] eyes of / did not do what was right in the sight of / did not do what the LORD his God said was right; his ancestor
decisions.reason: The good verdict is worded the same way at each level throughout Kings, here with "not". Balanced and Readable say "ancestor" for "father", as they do wherever David is called the father of a later king.

records.source: וַיֵּ֕לֶךְ בְּדֶ֖רֶךְ מַלְכֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְגַ֤ם אֶת־בְּנוֹ֙ הֶעֱבִ֣יר בָּאֵ֔שׁ כְּתֹֽעֲבוֹת֙ הַגּוֹיִ֔ם אֲשֶׁ֨ר הוֹרִ֤ישׁ יְהוָה֙ אֹתָ֔ם מִפְּנֵ֖י בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃
records.gloss: And he walked in [the] way of [the] kings of Israel, and even his son he made pass in the fire, according to [the] abominations of the nations whom dispossessed Yahweh from before [the] sons of Israel.
pieces: He walked in the way of the kings of Israel. He even made his son pass through the fire, following the detestable practices of the nations that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had driven out ahead of the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}}.

L.3: And he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, and he even made his son pass through the fire, according to the abominations of the nations whom {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had driven out before the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel.

R.3: He lived the way the kings of Israel had lived. He even burned his own son in the fire as a sacrifice. He copied the disgusting practices of the nations that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had driven out of the land ahead of the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}}.

decisions.choice: walked in the way of the kings of Israel: followed the northern kings in their worship
decisions.reason: To walk in someone's way is to live as they did. The kings of Israel worshiped at Jeroboam's shrines and, under Ahab, served Baal. Kings says the same of only two earlier kings of Judah, Jehoram and Ahaziah, who were related to Ahab by marriage (8:18, 27).

decisions.choice: made his son pass through the fire: burned his son as an offering
decisions.reason: The phrase names the rite of offering a child by fire to a god. 2 Chronicles 28:3 says of Ahaz that he "burned his sons in the fire", and Jeremiah 7:31 speaks of burning sons and daughters in the fire. Some have thought the phrase could mean a rite of passing a child through fire to dedicate it without killing it, but these passages point to a burnt sacrifice. Ahaz's grandson Manasseh did the same (21:6), and the northern kingdom too (17:17).

decisions.choice: the abominations of the nations: the practices Deuteronomy forbids
decisions.reason: Deuteronomy 18:9-10 warns Israel not to learn "the abominations of those nations" and forbids first of all anyone "who makes his son or his daughter pass through the fire" (also Deuteronomy 12:31). Ahaz does what the law named first among those abominations.

decisions.choice: the nations whom Yahweh drove out: the peoples Israel replaced
decisions.reason: Yahweh drove out the peoples of Canaan because of such practices (Deuteronomy 18:12). The king of Judah now takes up the very ways for which those nations lost the land, as was said of Judah under Rehoboam (1 Kings 14:24).

decisions.choice: burned his own son in the fire as a sacrifice
decisions.reason: Readable says what "pass through the fire" meant (m2), as it does at Deuteronomy 18:10. Literal and Balanced keep the Hebrew phrase.

decisions.choice: abominations (Literal); detestable practices (Balanced); disgusting practices (Readable)
decisions.reason: The word names what Yahweh finds loathsome. The wording follows 1 Kings 14:24.

records.source: וַיְזַבֵּ֧חַ וַיְקַטֵּ֛ר בַּבָּמ֖וֹת וְעַל־הַגְּבָע֑וֹת וְתַ֖חַת כָּל־עֵ֥ץ רַעֲנָֽן׃
records.gloss: And he sacrificed and made smoke at the high places and on the hills and under every tree luxuriant.
pieces: He offered sacrifices and burned incense at the high places, on the hills and under every leafy tree.

L.4: And he sacrificed and burned incense at the high places and on the hills and under every leafy tree.

R.4: He offered sacrifices and burned incense at the hilltop shrines, on the hills, and under every large, leafy tree.

decisions.choice: made smoke: burned incense or offerings
decisions.reason: The verb means to make something go up in smoke, either incense or parts of an offering. Beside "sacrificed" it describes the worship at the shrines, as at 1 Kings 22:44.

decisions.choice: on the hills and under every leafy tree: the places where the nations worshiped
decisions.reason: Deuteronomy 12:2 orders Israel to destroy the places where the nations served their gods "on the high mountains and on the hills and under every leafy tree". Judah built such places under Rehoboam (1 Kings 14:23), and the phrase is used again of Israel's worship (17:10).

decisions.choice: he sacrificed: the king himself, not only the people
decisions.reason: Under the good kings before him "the people" still sacrificed at the high places (15:4, 35). Now the king takes part himself.

decisions.choice: high places (Literal, Balanced); hilltop shrines (Readable); leafy tree
decisions.reason: The wording kept for these words in these books, as at 1 Kings 14:23.

records.source: אָ֣ז יַעֲלֶ֣ה רְצִ֣ין מֶֽלֶךְ־אֲ֠רָם וּפֶ֨קַח בֶּן־רְמַלְיָ֧הוּ מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם לַמִּלְחָמָ֑ה וַיָּצֻ֨רוּ֙ עַל־אָחָ֔ז וְלֹ֥א יָכְל֖וּ לְהִלָּחֵֽם׃
records.gloss: Then came up Rezin king of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel [to] Jerusalem for battle, and they besieged Ahaz, and not they were able to do battle.
pieces: Then Rezin king of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, came up to Jerusalem to make war. They besieged Ahaz, but they were not able to take the city.

L.5: Then Rezin king of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, came up [to] Jerusalem for battle, and they besieged Ahaz, but they were not able to fight [it out].

R.5: Then King Rezin of Aram and King Pekah son of Remaliah, who ruled Israel, came to attack Jerusalem. They surrounded Ahaz in the city, but they could not capture it.

decisions.choice: the same attack told in Isaiah 7:1
decisions.reason: Isaiah 7:1 opens with nearly the same words. The differences are small: Isaiah adds "against it" after "for battle", leaves out "they besieged Ahaz", and has "he was not able to fight against it" where Kings has the plural, "they were not able to fight". The wording here follows the translation of Isaiah 7:1 where the Hebrew is the same. Isaiah 7:2-9 tells how the prophet urged Ahaz to stay calm and trust Yahweh during this attack.

decisions.choice: Rezin and Pekah: an alliance against Judah
decisions.reason: Rezin ruled Aram from Damascus and Pekah ruled Israel from Samaria. In the 730s BC, as Assyria pressed west, they marched on Jerusalem; Isaiah 7:6 says they planned to put a king of their own choosing, "the son of Tabeel", on Judah's throne. 2 Chronicles 28:5-8 tells of heavy losses Judah suffered in this war.

decisions.choice: they besieged Ahaz: they shut him up in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: To besiege a king is to surround the city he is in. The king, not only the city, was the target of the attack.

decisions.choice: not able to fight: not able to win the battle
decisions.reason: "Fight" here means to fight the battle through to the end, that is, to take the city. Isaiah 7:1 uses the same verb in this sense.

decisions.choice: take the city / capture it
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "fight" means here (m4), as Isaiah 7:1 does. Readable says "King Rezin" and "King Pekah" and "who ruled Israel", as Isaiah 7:1 does; it leaves out "northern kingdom" there, since Kings uses "Israel" for that kingdom throughout.

records.source: בָּעֵ֣ת הַהִ֗יא הֵ֠שִׁיב רְצִ֨ין מֶֽלֶךְ־אֲרָ֤ם אֶת־אֵילַת֙ לַֽאֲרָ֔ם וַיְנַשֵּׁ֥ל אֶת־הַיְהוּדִ֖ים מֵֽאֵיל֑וֹת וַֽאֲדוֹמִים֙בָּ֣אוּ אֵילַ֔ת וַיֵּ֣שְׁבוּ שָׁ֔ם עַ֖ד הַיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּֽה׃פ
records.gloss: At the time the that restored Rezin king of Aram Elath to Aram, and he cleared out the Judeans from Eloth; and Edomites came [to] Elath, and they have lived there until the day the this.
pieces: At that time Rezin king of Aram recovered Elath for Aram and drove the people of Judah out of Elath. Edomites came to Elath, and they have lived there to this day.

L.6: At that time Rezin king of Aram restored Elath to Aram, and he drove the Judeans out of Elath; and Edomites came [to] Elath, and they have lived there to this day.

R.6: At that time King Rezin of Aram took back the town of Elath for Aram and drove out the people of Judah who lived there. Then Edomites moved into Elath, and they live there to this day.

decisions.choice: Edomites: the reading of the Hebrew tradition; "Aram" kept earlier in the verse
alternatives: the king of Edom recovered Elath for Edom
Arameans came to Elath (the written text)
decisions.reason: The written Hebrew text reads "Arameans" at the end of the verse; the tradition of reading it aloud reads "Edomites", which is followed here. In Hebrew the names Aram and Edom differ by only one letter, and two letters that look much alike. Elath lay at the head of the gulf of the Red Sea, far from Aram and next to Edom, and it had been taken from Edom (14:7, 22). For this reason many think the verse first said that the king of Edom recovered Elath "for Edom", and that "Rezin king of Aram" and "Aram" came in through copying. Every level keeps the Hebrew "Rezin king of Aram ... for Aram"; reviewers should check the evidence.

decisions.choice: Elath: Judah's port on the Red Sea
decisions.reason: Elath stood at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba, near Ezion-geber where Solomon kept his ships (1 Kings 9:26). Azariah of Judah had rebuilt it and restored it to Judah (14:22). "Restored" here takes up that word: Elath now changes hands again. Losing it cut Judah off from the trade of the Red Sea.

decisions.choice: the Judeans: the people of Judah
decisions.reason: This is the first time the word for "Judeans", later "Jews", appears in the Hebrew Bible. Here it means the people of the kingdom of Judah who lived in Elath.

decisions.choice: to this day: the writer's own time
decisions.reason: As at 2:22, "to this day" means up to the time when the account was written: Elath was still in Edomite hands then.

decisions.choice: the people of Judah
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "the people of Judah" so that readers do not take the word in its later sense of the Jewish people as a whole. Literal keeps "Judeans".

records.source: וַיִּשְׁלַ֨ח אָחָ֜ז מַלְאָכִ֗ים אֶל־תִּ֠גְלַת פְּלֶ֤סֶר מֶֽלֶךְ־אַשּׁוּר֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר עַבְדְּךָ֥ וּבִנְךָ֖ אָ֑נִי עֲלֵ֨ה וְהוֹשִׁעֵ֜נִי מִכַּ֣ף מֶֽלֶךְ־אֲרָ֗ם וּמִכַּף֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל הַקּוֹמִ֖ים עָלָֽי׃
records.gloss: And sent Ahaz messengers to Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, saying, your servant and your son [am] I; come up and save me from [the] palm of [the] king of Aram and from [the] palm of [the] king of Israel, the [ones] rising up against me.
pieces: Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria with this message: "I am your servant and your son. Come up and rescue me from the power of the king of Aram and the king of Israel, who are attacking me."

L.7: And Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, saying, "Your servant and your son [am] I. Come up and save me from the hand of the king of Aram and from the hand of the king of Israel, who are rising up against me."

R.7: Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser, the king of Assyria, with this message: "I am your servant and your son. Come and save me from the king of Aram and the king of Israel. They are attacking me."

decisions.choice: Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria
decisions.reason: Tiglath-pileser III ruled Assyria from 745 to 727 BC and pushed its empire west to the Mediterranean. He is also called Pul (15:19), and he had already taken towns of northern Israel in Pekah's reign (15:29).

decisions.choice: your servant and your son: the words of a vassal to his overlord
decisions.reason: A king who calls himself another king's servant and son places himself under him as a subject king, owing loyalty and tribute. Ahaz offers Judah's submission to Assyria in return for help.

decisions.choice: son ... save me: help sought from Assyria rather than from Yahweh
decisions.reason: Yahweh had promised that David's heir would be a son to him (2 Samuel 7:14), and through Isaiah he told Ahaz not to fear these two kings but to trust him (Isaiah 7:4, 9). Ahaz instead calls himself the Assyrian king's son and asks him to save.

decisions.choice: from the palm of: from the power of
decisions.reason: The hand or palm stands for power or control. Rising up against someone means attacking him.

decisions.choice: your servant at every level
decisions.reason: As in other polite or submissive self-references, "your servant" stands at every level. Here it is the formal language of a subject king (m2), and "slave" would suggest a household slave rather than a vassal.

decisions.choice: save me from the king of Aram and the king of Israel. They are attacking me.
decisions.reason: Readable leaves out the picture of the hand (m4) and puts "rising up against me" in a sentence of its own.

records.heading: Ahaz turns to Assyria

records.source: וַיִּקַּ֨ח אָחָ֜ז אֶת־הַכֶּ֣סֶף וְאֶת־הַזָּהָ֗ב הַנִּמְצָא֙ בֵּ֣ית יְהוָ֔ה וּבְאֹֽצְר֖וֹת בֵּ֣ית הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וַיִּשְׁלַ֥ח לְמֶֽלֶךְ־אַשּׁ֖וּר שֹֽׁחַד׃
records.gloss: And took Ahaz the silver and the gold found [in the] house of Yahweh and in [the] treasuries of [the] house of the king, and he sent to [the] king of Assyria a bribe.
pieces: Ahaz took the silver and gold to be found in the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and in the palace treasuries, and he sent it as a bribe to the king of Assyria.

L.8: And Ahaz took the silver and the gold that was found in the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and in the treasuries of the house of the king, and he sent [it] to the king of Assyria [as] a bribe.

R.8: Ahaz took the silver and gold that was in the temple of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and in the treasure rooms of the royal palace. He sent it to the king of Assyria as a bribe.

decisions.choice: bribe: a payment to buy someone's action
decisions.reason: The word is the one used for a bribe that bends a judge (Exodus 23:8; Deuteronomy 16:19), not a friendly gift. Asa used the same word when he paid Ben-hadad to break a treaty (1 Kings 15:19). Ahaz buys Assyria's help with the temple's wealth.

decisions.choice: emptying the treasuries: as Asa and Jehoash had done
decisions.reason: Asa sent the treasures of the temple and the palace to Damascus to buy help against Israel (1 Kings 15:18), and Jehoash of Judah paid off Hazael with them (12:19). Now Ahaz pays Assyria to strike Damascus.

decisions.choice: found: what was there
decisions.reason: "Found" means whatever was on hand at the time in the temple and the royal treasuries.

decisions.choice: the temple of the LORD; treasure rooms of the royal palace
decisions.reason: Readable says "temple" for the house of Yahweh and "royal palace" for the house of the king, as these books do.

records.source: וַיִּשְׁמַ֤ע אֵלָיו֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֔וּר וַיַּעַל֩ מֶ֨לֶךְ אַשּׁ֤וּר אֶל־דַּמֶּ֨שֶׂק֙ וַֽיִּתְפְּשֶׂ֔הָ וַיַּגְלֶ֖הָ קִ֑ירָה וְאֶת־רְצִ֖ין הֵמִֽית׃
records.gloss: And listened to him [the] king of Assyria, and went up [the] king of Assyria to Damascus and seized it, and he exiled it [to] Kir, and Rezin he put to death.
pieces: The king of Assyria agreed to his request. He marched up against Damascus and captured it. He took its people into exile to Kir and put Rezin to death.

L.9: And the king of Assyria listened to him, and the king of Assyria went up against Damascus and seized it, and he carried it [into exile to] Kir, and he put Rezin to death.

R.9: The king of Assyria agreed to help Ahaz. He attacked Damascus and captured it. He forced its people to move to Kir as captives, and he killed Rezin.

decisions.choice: listened to him: agreed to his request
decisions.reason: To listen to a request is to agree to it and act on it, as at 1 Kings 15:20.

decisions.choice: the fall of Damascus: the end of the kingdom of Aram
decisions.reason: Damascus fell to Assyria in 732 BC. Its king was killed and its land became part of the Assyrian empire. Isaiah had foretold that Damascus would be plundered before the child of the sign could speak (Isaiah 8:4; 7:16).

decisions.choice: Kir: where the Arameans came from
decisions.reason: Amos had foretold that the people of Aram would go into exile to Kir (Amos 1:5), and he names Kir as the place from which Yahweh brought the Arameans (Amos 9:7). They are sent back where their history began. Where Kir lay is not known.

decisions.choice: exiled it: carried off its people
decisions.reason: "It" refers to the city, meaning its people. Assyria moved conquered peoples to distant lands to break their resistance (17:6).

decisions.choice: its people
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say who was carried off (m4). Readable also says "agreed to help Ahaz" and explains exile as being forced to move as captives.

records.source: וַיֵּ֣לֶךְ הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אָחָ֡ז לִ֠קְרַאת תִּגְלַ֨ת פִּלְאֶ֤סֶר מֶֽלֶךְ־אַשּׁוּר֙ דּוּמֶּ֔שֶׂק וַיַּ֥רְא אֶת־הַמִּזְבֵּ֖חַ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בְּדַמָּ֑שֶׂק וַיִּשְׁלַח֩ הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ אָחָ֜ז אֶל־אוּרִיָּ֣ה הַכֹּהֵ֗ן אֶת־דְּמ֧וּת הַמִּזְבֵּ֛חַ וְאֶת־תַּבְנִית֖וֹ לְכָֽל־מַעֲשֵֽׂהוּ׃
records.gloss: And went the king Ahaz to meet Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria [at] Damascus, and he saw the altar which [was] in Damascus; and sent the king Ahaz to Uriah the priest [the] likeness of the altar and its pattern, for all its workmanship.
pieces: King Ahaz went to meet Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria at Damascus. There he saw the altar that stood in Damascus. Then King Ahaz sent Uriah the priest a model and a design of the altar, with all the details of how it was made.

L.10: And King Ahaz went to meet Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria [at] Damascus, and he saw the altar that [was] in Damascus. And King Ahaz sent to Uriah the priest the likeness of the altar and its pattern, for all its workmanship.

R.10: King Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglath-pileser, the king of Assyria. While he was there, he saw the altar in Damascus. He sent Uriah the priest a model of the altar and a plan that showed exactly how it was made.

decisions.choice: went to meet the king of Assyria: a subject king presenting himself
decisions.reason: Ahaz goes to the conquered city of Damascus to appear before his new overlord, as subject kings were required to do.

decisions.choice: the altar in Damascus: a foreign altar
decisions.reason: The text does not say whose altar it was, an Aramean one or one the Assyrians set up, or to which god it belonged. What matters to the writer is that the new altar of Yahweh's temple is copied from it.

decisions.choice: likeness and pattern: a design from Damascus instead of from Yahweh
decisions.reason: The word "pattern" is the one used for the pattern of the tabernacle and its furnishings that Yahweh showed Moses (Exodus 25:9, 40), and for the plan of the temple David gave Solomon (1 Chronicles 28:11-19). Here the pattern for the altar comes from a foreign city.

decisions.choice: Uriah the priest: the chief priest at the temple
decisions.reason: Uriah appears to be the leading priest in Jerusalem. Isaiah names "Uriah the priest" as a reliable witness (Isaiah 8:2), most likely the same man.

decisions.choice: a model ... its design / a plan; with all the details of how it was made
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "model" for "likeness" and "design" or "plan" for "pattern", and turn "for all its workmanship" into a plain phrase. Readable adds "While he was there" to link the two events.

records.source: וַיִּ֛בֶן אוּרִיָּ֥ה הַכֹּהֵ֖ן אֶת־הַמִּזְבֵּ֑חַ כְּכֹ֣ל אֲשֶׁר־שָׁלַח֩ הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ אָחָ֜ז מִדַּמֶּ֗שֶׂק כֵּ֤ן עָשָׂה֙ אוּרִיָּ֣ה הַכֹּהֵ֔ן עַד־בּ֥וֹא הַמֶּֽלֶךְ־אָחָ֖ז מִדַּמָּֽשֶׂק׃
records.gloss: And built Uriah the priest the altar according to all that had sent the king Ahaz from Damascus; so did Uriah the priest until [the] coming of the king Ahaz from Damascus.
pieces: Uriah the priest built the altar following everything King Ahaz had sent from Damascus. He had it finished by the time King Ahaz came back from Damascus.

L.11: And Uriah the priest built the altar according to all that King Ahaz had sent from Damascus; so Uriah the priest did, until King Ahaz came from Damascus.

R.11: Uriah the priest built the altar exactly like the model and plan King Ahaz had sent from Damascus. He finished it before King Ahaz came home.

decisions.choice: so Uriah did until the king came: the work was done before the king returned
decisions.reason: The second half of the verse repeats that Uriah followed the king's instructions, and adds that he did so in the time before Ahaz came back. The altar was ready when he arrived (verse 12).

decisions.choice: according to all that the king had sent: the priest follows the king's design
decisions.reason: The words "according to all that" are used of the builders of the tabernacle, who made everything as Yahweh had commanded Moses (Exodus 39:42). Here the priest builds by the king's command, from a pattern that came from Damascus (verse 10).

decisions.choice: had it finished by the time ... came back / finished it before ... came home
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say plainly what "so he did until the king came" means (m1). Readable also says "the model and plan" for "all that the king had sent" (verse 10).

records.source: וַיָּבֹ֤א הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ מִדַּמֶּ֔שֶׂק וַיַּ֥רְא הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ אֶת־הַמִּזְבֵּ֑חַ וַיִּקְרַ֥ב הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ עַל־הַמִּזְבֵּ֖חַ וַיַּ֥עַל עָלָֽיו׃
records.gloss: And came the king from Damascus, and saw the king the altar, and drew near the king to the altar, and he offered up on it.
pieces: On his return from Damascus the king saw the altar; he approached it and offered sacrifices on it.

L.12: And the king came from Damascus, and the king saw the altar, and the king drew near to the altar and offered [sacrifices] on it.

R.12: The king came home from Damascus and saw the altar. He went up to it and offered sacrifices on it.

decisions.choice: offered on it: or "went up on it"
decisions.reason: The Hebrew letters can be read as "he went up on it", climbing the altar's steps or ramp, or as "he offered up on it", making offerings rise on it. The vowels of the Hebrew text give "offered up", and verse 13 says what he offered. Either way Ahaz himself served at the altar.

decisions.choice: the king at the altar: Ahaz acts as priest
decisions.reason: The word "king" is repeated three times: it is the king who sees, approaches and offers. Kings had offered sacrifices at great occasions before (1 Kings 8:62-64), but Jeroboam's offering at his own altar is the closest parallel (1 Kings 12:33). 2 Chronicles 26:16-21 tells how Uzziah was struck with skin disease for burning incense in the temple.

decisions.choice: On his return ... the king saw the altar; he approached it ... / The king came home ... He went up to it ...
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable join the four short clauses into fewer sentences and say "the king" once. Literal keeps the repetition.

decisions.choice: sacrifices
decisions.reason: The verb has no object; English needs one. Literal puts it in brackets.

records.source: וַיַּקְטֵ֤ר אֶת־עֹֽלָתוֹ֙ וְאֶת־מִנְחָת֔וֹ וַיַּסֵּ֖ךְ אֶת־נִסְכּ֑וֹ וַיִּזְרֹ֛ק אֶת־דַּֽם־הַשְּׁלָמִ֥ים אֲשֶׁר־ל֖וֹ עַל־הַמִּזְבֵּֽחַ׃
records.gloss: And he made smoke his burnt offering and his grain offering, and he poured out his drink offering, and he dashed [the] blood of the peace offerings which [were] his on the altar.
pieces: He burned his burnt offering and grain offering, poured his drink offering, and splashed the blood of his peace offerings on the altar.

L.13: And he burned his burnt offering and his grain offering, and he poured out his drink offering, and he dashed the blood of his peace offerings on the altar.

R.13: He burned his burnt offering and his grain offering on it. He poured out his drink offering and splashed the blood of his peace offerings on the altar.

decisions.choice: burnt, grain, drink and peace offerings: the offerings that dedicate an altar
decisions.reason: These are the main kinds of offering in the law (Leviticus 1-3; Numbers 15:1-10). Offered together, they put the new altar into use, as Solomon's offerings did at the dedication of the temple (1 Kings 8:64).

decisions.choice: his ... which were his: the king's own offerings
decisions.reason: Each offering is called "his", and the peace offerings "which were his". These were the king's own offerings, not the people's.

decisions.choice: dashed: threw the blood against the altar
decisions.reason: The verb means to throw or splash a liquid. The blood of the offerings was thrown against the altar (Leviticus 3:2).

decisions.choice: dashed (Literal); splashed (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "splashed", as Leviticus 3:2 does; Literal keeps "dashed". Readable adds "on it" after the first clause so that every offering is placed on the new altar.

records.source: וְאֵ֨ת הַמִּזְבַּ֣ח הַנְּחֹשֶׁת֮ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לִפְנֵ֣י יְהוָה֒ וַיַּקְרֵ֗ב מֵאֵת֙ פְּנֵ֣י הַבַּ֔יִת מִבֵּין֙ הַמִּזְבֵּ֔חַ וּמִבֵּ֖ין בֵּ֣ית יְהוָ֑ה וַיִּתֵּ֥ן אֹת֛וֹ עַל־יֶ֥רֶךְ הַמִּזְבֵּ֖חַ צָפֽוֹנָה׃
records.gloss: And the altar the bronze which [was] before Yahweh, and he brought [it] near from with [the] front of the house, from between the altar and from between [the] house of Yahweh, and he put it on [the] side of the altar northward.
pieces: As for the bronze altar that stood before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, he moved it from the front of the temple, from its place between the new altar and the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and set it beside the new altar on the north.

L.14: And the bronze altar that [was] before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, he brought [it] from the front of the house, from between the altar and the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and he put it on the north side of the altar.

R.14: There was also the bronze altar that stood in front of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. It stood between the new altar and the temple of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. Ahaz moved it away from the front of the temple and put it on the north side of the new altar.

decisions.choice: the bronze altar that was before Yahweh: Solomon's altar
decisions.reason: This is the bronze altar Solomon made for the court in front of the temple, called by the same words at 1 Kings 8:64 (2 Chronicles 4:1). It stood before the temple entrance, where the offerings to Yahweh were made.

decisions.choice: brought it from between the altar and the house: moved it out of the way
decisions.reason: Ahaz's new altar seems to have been set up in front of the old one, east of it, so that the bronze altar stood between the new altar and the temple. Ahaz "brought it near", that is, moved it from that central place to the north side. The Hebrew puts the bronze altar first in the sentence, before the verb, to show that the verse now turns to it.

decisions.choice: before Yahweh ... the house of Yahweh: the altar of Yahweh pushed aside
decisions.reason: The divine name is repeated: the bronze altar stood before Yahweh, in front of his house. The new altar from Damascus now takes its place.

decisions.choice: the new altar
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says only "the altar". Balanced and Readable add "new" to tell the two altars apart. Readable puts the verse in three sentences and names Ahaz.

records.source: וַיְצַוֶּ֣ה הַמֶּֽלֶךְ־אָ֠חָז אֶת־אוּרִיָּ֨ה הַכֹּהֵ֜ן לֵאמֹ֗ר עַ֣ל הַמִּזְבֵּ֣חַ הַגָּד֡וֹל הַקְטֵ֣ר אֶת־עֹֽלַת־הַבֹּקֶר֩ וְאֶת־מִנְחַ֨ת הָעֶ֜רֶב וְֽאֶת־עֹלַ֧ת הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ וְאֶת־מִנְחָת֗וֹ וְ֠אֵת עֹלַ֞ת כָּל־עַ֤ם הָאָ֨רֶץ֙ וּמִנְחָתָ֣ם וְנִסְכֵּיהֶ֔ם וְכָל־דַּ֥ם עֹלָ֛ה וְכָל־דַּם־זֶ֖בַח עָלָ֣יו תִּזְרֹ֑ק וּמִזְבַּ֧ח הַנְּחֹ֛שֶׁת יִֽהְיֶה־לִּ֖י לְבַקֵּֽר׃
records.gloss: And commanded the king Ahaz Uriah the priest, saying, on the altar the great make smoke [the] burnt offering of the morning and [the] grain offering of the evening and [the] burnt offering of the king and his grain offering and [the] burnt offering of all [the] people of the land and their grain offering and their drink offerings, and all [the] blood of burnt offering and all [the] blood of sacrifice on it you will dash; and [the] altar of the bronze will be for me to inquire.
pieces: Then King Ahaz gave orders to Uriah the priest: "On the great altar burn the morning burnt offering and the evening grain offering, the king's burnt offering and his grain offering, and the burnt offering of all the people of the land with their grain offerings and drink offerings. Splash on it all the blood of the burnt offerings and of the sacrifices. But the bronze altar will be for me to seek guidance by."

L.15: And King Ahaz commanded Uriah the priest, saying, "On the great altar burn the morning burnt offering and the evening grain offering, and the burnt offering of the king and his grain offering, and the burnt offering of all the people of the land and their grain offering and their drink offerings; and all the blood of [the] burnt offering and all the blood of [the] sacrifice you shall dash on it. And the bronze altar shall be for me to inquire [by]."

R.15: Then King Ahaz gave Uriah the priest these orders: "Use the great new altar for all the offerings: the burnt offering in the morning and the grain offering in the evening, the king's burnt offering and grain offering, and the burnt offerings, grain offerings and drink offerings that all the people of the land bring. Splash all the blood of the burnt offerings and the other sacrifices on this altar. But I will use the bronze altar to seek guidance."

decisions.choice: commanded: the reading of the Hebrew tradition
decisions.reason: The written Hebrew has "commanded him", with a pronoun that points ahead to Uriah; the tradition of reading it aloud reads "commanded" alone. The meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: the morning burnt offering and the evening grain offering: the daily offerings
decisions.reason: The law set a burnt offering every morning and evening, each with grain and drink offerings (Exodus 29:38-42; Numbers 28:3-8). Kings names "the offering" at the evening hour (1 Kings 18:29, 36). All the regular worship is now to be done at the new altar.

decisions.choice: the people of the land: the citizens of Judah
decisions.reason: "The people of the land" are the free landowning people of Judah, who had a voice in national affairs (11:14, 18-20). Their offerings, like the king's, are moved to the new altar.

decisions.choice: the bronze altar shall be for me to inquire by: for the king to seek guidance
alternatives: the bronze altar will be for me to consider (what to do with it)
decisions.reason: The verb means to look into or examine something closely (Leviticus 13:36; 27:33), and to seek God in his temple (Psalm 27:4). Ahaz may mean that he will use the old altar to seek a word from God, perhaps by examining the parts of sacrifices for signs, as the peoples around Israel did. Or he may mean only that he will consider later what to do with it. The words are brief, and the sense is not certain.

decisions.choice: the great altar: the new altar from Damascus
decisions.reason: "The great altar" is the new one, larger than Solomon's bronze altar, which had already proved too small for great occasions (1 Kings 8:64).

decisions.choice: Use the great new altar for all the offerings: ...
decisions.reason: Readable starts with what Ahaz wants and then lists the offerings, and it adds "new" (verse 14). It puts the people's offerings together in one phrase.

decisions.choice: splash; seek guidance
decisions.reason: "Splash" as in verse 13. "Seek guidance" says what "inquire" means in the reading followed here (m4). Balanced and Readable say "But" because the bronze altar is set against the great altar.

records.source: וַיַּ֖עַשׂ אוּרִיָּ֣ה הַכֹּהֵ֑ן כְּכֹ֥ל אֲשֶׁר־צִוָּ֖ה הַמֶּ֥לֶךְ אָחָֽז׃
records.gloss: And did Uriah the priest according to all that commanded the king Ahaz.
pieces: Uriah the priest did everything King Ahaz commanded.

L.16: And Uriah the priest did according to all that King Ahaz commanded.

R.16: Uriah the priest did everything King Ahaz told him to do.

decisions.choice: did according to all that the king commanded: the priest obeys the king
decisions.reason: The words echo the way Moses and Israel did "according to all that Yahweh commanded" (Exodus 39:42). The priest of Yahweh's temple now carries out the king's commands without question, unlike the priest Jehoiada, who led the overthrow of Athaliah (chapter 11).

records.source: וַיְקַצֵּץ֩ הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ אָחָ֜ז אֶת־הַמִּסְגְּר֣וֹת הַמְּכֹנ֗וֹת וַיָּ֤סַר מֵֽעֲלֵיהֶם֙ אֶת־הַכִּיֹּ֔ר וְאֶת־הַיָּ֣ם הוֹרִ֔ד מֵעַ֛ל הַבָּקָ֥ר הַנְּחֹ֖שֶׁת אֲשֶׁ֣ר תַּחְתֶּ֑יהָ וַיִּתֵּ֣ן אֹת֔וֹ עַ֖ל מַרְצֶ֥פֶת אֲבָנִֽים׃
records.gloss: And cut off the king Ahaz the panels of the stands, and he removed from on them the basin; and the sea he took down from on the oxen the bronze which [were] under it, and he put it on a pavement of stones.
pieces: King Ahaz cut off the panels of the stands and removed the basins from them. He took the Sea down from the bronze oxen that held it up and set it on a stone pavement.

L.17: And King Ahaz cut off the panels of the stands and removed the basin from on them; and he took down the sea from on the bronze oxen that [were] under it, and he put it on a pavement of stones.

R.17: King Ahaz cut off the side panels of the stands and took the basins off them. He also took the huge bronze tank called the Sea down from the bronze oxen that held it up, and he set it on a base made of stones.

decisions.choice: the stands, the basins and the Sea: Solomon's bronze furnishings
decisions.reason: These were made for Solomon's temple: ten bronze stands on wheels, each with panels on its sides and a basin on top, and the great bronze basin called the Sea, which rested on twelve bronze oxen (1 Kings 7:23-39). The Sea is not a body of water but a great tank.

decisions.choice: why Ahaz stripped them: probably for their bronze
alternatives: to change the temple to suit the new altar
decisions.reason: The text gives no reason here. Verse 18 ends "because of the king of Assyria", and the bronze may have been needed for tribute to Assyria. The oxen were later carried off by the Babylonians (Jeremiah 52:20).

decisions.choice: the basin: each basin, all ten
decisions.reason: "The basin" is singular, but it refers to the basin on each of the stands (1 Kings 7:38).

decisions.choice: basins
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "basins", since there was one on each stand (m3). Readable explains the Sea as a huge bronze tank, as at 1 Kings 7:23, and says "side panels" as at 1 Kings 7:28.

records.source: וְאֶת־מוּסַ֨ךְ הַשַּׁבָּ֜ת אֲשֶׁר־בָּנ֣וּ בַבַּ֗יִת וְאֶת־מְב֤וֹא הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ הַֽחִיצ֔וֹנָה הֵסֵ֖ב בֵּ֣ית יְהוָ֑ה מִפְּנֵ֖י מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר׃
records.gloss: And [the] covered [structure] of the Sabbath which they had built in the house, and [the] entrance of the king the outer, he turned [from the] house of Yahweh because of [the] king of Assyria.
pieces: He also removed from the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} the covered place for the Sabbath that had been built at the temple, and the king's outer entrance. He did this because of the king of Assyria.

L.18: And the covered [structure] of the Sabbath that they had built in the house, and the outer entrance of the king, he turned [away from] the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} because of the king of Assyria.

R.18: He also took away from the temple of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} the covered place used on the Sabbath that had been built there, and the king's outside entrance. He did this because of the king of Assyria.

decisions.choice: the covered structure of the Sabbath: something covered, used on the Sabbath
alternatives: the covered walkway for the Sabbath
the base of the (royal) seat (Greek translation)
decisions.reason: The word comes from a root meaning "to cover" and is found only here. It may have been a covered walkway, or a covered platform or stand where the king sat or stood at the Sabbath gatherings (compare 11:14). The written Hebrew spells the word differently from the way the tradition reads it aloud, and the ancient Greek translation seems to have read "the base of the seat". What it was exactly is not known; reviewers should check the evidence.

decisions.choice: the outer entrance of the king: the king's own way into the temple
decisions.reason: This was a private entrance from the palace into the temple area, used by the king, as the palace stood beside the temple.

decisions.choice: he turned from the house of Yahweh: removed, or changed
alternatives: he changed them in the house of Yahweh
he moved them around the house of Yahweh
decisions.reason: The verb means "to turn" or "to cause to go around". With the house of Yahweh it most likely means that Ahaz removed these things from the temple. It may instead mean that he altered them or turned them around within the temple area.

decisions.choice: because of the king of Assyria: to satisfy his overlord
decisions.reason: The text does not say exactly why. Ahaz may have removed signs of royal power and independence that would offend his overlord, or taken materials to pay tribute (verse 17). Either way, the changes to Yahweh's house were made out of regard for the king of Assyria.

decisions.choice: He also removed ... He did this because of the king of Assyria.
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Hebrew order, with the objects first. Balanced and Readable put the verb first and give the reason in a sentence of its own. They say "the covered place", keeping the wording general because the object is not known (m1).

records.source: וְיֶ֛תֶר דִּבְרֵ֥י אָחָ֖ז אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָשָׂ֑ה הֲלֹא־הֵ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים עַל־סֵ֛פֶר דִּבְרֵ֥י הַיָּמִ֖ים לְמַלְכֵ֥י יְהוּדָֽה׃
records.gloss: And [the] rest of [the] matters of Ahaz which he did, [are] not they written on [the] book of [the] matters of the days of [the] kings of Judah?
pieces: The rest of the acts of Ahaz, what he did, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Judah.

L.19: And the rest of the matters of Ahaz that he did, are they not written in the book of the matters of the days of the kings of Judah?

R.19: Everything else Ahaz did is written in the history of the kings of Judah.

decisions.choice: the book of the matters of the days of the kings of Judah: a royal record the writer used
decisions.reason: As at 8:23, the writer sends the reader to a fuller record of the reigns of Judah's kings, now lost. The question "are they not written ...?" means "they are written".

decisions.choice: more about Ahaz in Chronicles and Isaiah
decisions.reason: 2 Chronicles 28 tells of further defeats in Ahaz's reign and of his closing the doors of the temple (28:24). Isaiah 7 tells of his meeting with the prophet during the attack of verse 5.

decisions.choice: a statement at Balanced and Readable
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the question; Balanced and Readable state the fact, as throughout Kings.

records.source: וַיִּשְׁכַּ֤ב אָחָז֙ עִם־אֲבֹתָ֔יו וַיִּקָּבֵ֥ר עִם־אֲבֹתָ֖יו בְּעִ֣יר דָּוִ֑ד וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ חִזְקִיָּ֥הוּ בְנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו׃פ
records.gloss: And lay down Ahaz with his fathers, and he was buried with his fathers in [the] city of David, and reigned Hezekiah his son in his place.
pieces: Then Ahaz rested with his ancestors and was buried with them in the City of David. His son Hezekiah became king in his place.

L.20: And Ahaz lay down with his fathers, and he was buried with his fathers in the City of David, and Hezekiah his son reigned in his place.

R.20: Then Ahaz died and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David. His son Hezekiah became king after him.

decisions.choice: lay down with his fathers: died
decisions.reason: The death formula of Kings (1 Kings 15:8, 24). Here the Hebrew also names his burial "with his fathers" in the City of David.

decisions.choice: buried in the City of David: 2 Chronicles adds a difference
decisions.reason: 2 Chronicles 28:27 says that Ahaz was buried in the city, in Jerusalem, but was not brought into the tombs of the kings of Israel. Kings says only that he was buried with his fathers in the City of David.

decisions.choice: Hezekiah his son
decisions.reason: Hezekiah's reign is told in chapters 18-20, where he is praised as a king who trusted Yahweh as none before or after him (18:5).

decisions.choice: lay down with his fathers / rested with his ancestors / died ... and was buried with his ancestors
decisions.reason: The death formula is worded the same way at each level throughout Kings; Readable keeps the burial with his ancestors because the Hebrew names it.
